facts.patientLine: Just bathed it with cooled boiled water. Haven't put anything in it.

deflections: Sorry, could you say that another way?

Not sure. Ask me whatever helps.

patients.name: Erin Walsh
patients.chiefComplaint: Asking about teething remedies for her infant
patients.openingLine: Hi — my little one is teething and miserable. What can I give her? She's seven months.

facts.label: Age
facts.value: 29 (parent)
facts.patientLine: I'm 29 — it's my daughter who's unwell.

facts.label: Chief complaint
facts.value: Teething discomfort in a 7-month-old
facts.patientLine: She's seven months and she's been really unsettled. I think it's her teeth.

facts.label: Infant weight
facts.value: 8.2 kg, weighed at clinic last week
facts.patientLine: She was 8.2 kilos at the clinic last week.

facts.label: Duration
facts.value: 3 days of unsettled behaviour
facts.patientLine: About three days now. She's just not herself.

facts.label: Red flags
facts.value: No fever, feeding normally, wet nappies, no rash, rousable and alert
facts.patientLine: No temperature, she's feeding fine, nappies are wet, no rash. She's alert enough.

facts.label: Already given
facts.value: Infant paracetamol given twice yesterday; unsure of the dose used
facts.patientLine: I gave her some Calpol yesterday, twice. I'm not certain how much, I just used the spoon.

facts.label: Allergy
facts.value: No known allergies in the infant
facts.patientLine: None that we know of.

facts.label: Medical history
facts.value: Born at term, no medical problems, immunisations up to date
facts.patientLine: She was full term, no problems, and she's had all her jabs.

facts.label: Teething signs
facts.value: Drooling, gum rubbing, one tooth visible through the gum
facts.patientLine: She's drooling loads and chewing everything. I can see a tooth coming through.

facts.label: Products considered
facts.value: Was offered a teething gel by a friend; considering an amber necklace
facts.patientLine: A friend gave me a teething gel, and someone suggested one of those amber necklaces.

facts.label: Context
facts.value: First-time parent, limited sleep, anxious about doing the wrong thing
facts.patientLine: She's my first. I've barely slept and I'm scared of getting it wrong.

deflections: Sorry, I'm not sure what you're asking.
I don't think so — should I have checked that?
I'm not sure. Sorry, I'm quite tired.
impatientLines: Sorry, she's due a feed soon — is there something I can just take?
I've been up all night. Can you just tell me what to buy?

followUps.line: How much exactly, and how often? I don't want to give her too much.
So is the gel no good then? And the necklace — is that dangerous?
I've just been using the spoon from the kitchen drawer. Is that wrong?

scenarios.title: The Headache That Isn’t Simple
scenarios.tagline: A routine request that deserves a careful conversation.
scenarios.description: A 20-year-old walks in asking for something for a headache. Straightforward on the surface — but the right answer depends entirely on what you think to ask.
scenarios.mission:
A 20-year-old patient enters the pharmacy asking for something for a headache.

Your job is to determine whether self-care is appropriate.

The patient will not tell you everything automatically.

Ask the right questions.
objectives: Take a structured headache history, including onset, severity and character.
Screen actively for neurological and systemic red flags.
Uncover allergy, medication and relevant past medical history before recommending.
Choose an analgesic that is safe for this specific patient.
Counsel on dose, maximum daily dose and when to seek further help.

scenarios.title: The Persistent Cough
scenarios.tagline: Five weeks of coughing, and a request for “something strong”.
scenarios.description: A 58-year-old wants a stronger cough medicine. Deciding whether that is the right response means separating a self-limiting cough from one that needs investigation.
scenarios.mission:
A 58-year-old patient asks for a stronger cough medicine.

Decide whether an over-the-counter product is appropriate, or whether this cough needs someone else to see it.

The details that matter will not be offered unprompted.
objectives: Establish cough duration, character and associated symptoms.
Screen for weight loss, haemoptysis, night sweats and smoking history.
Consider medication-induced cough as a differential.
Reach a clear, justified referral decision and communicate its urgency.

scenarios.title: Heartburn After Dinner
scenarios.tagline: Antacids are not working. Find out why.
scenarios.description: Three months of evening reflux in a 41-year-old. The cause may already be in her medicine cabinet.
scenarios.mission:
A 41-year-old patient describes burning chest discomfort most evenings.

Work out what is driving it, whether alarm features are present, and what should happen next.
objectives: Characterise the reflux symptoms and their pattern.
Screen for alarm features requiring referral.
Identify the NSAID as a likely contributing cause.
Give lifestyle and treatment advice the patient can actually follow.

scenarios.title: Seasonal Allergy Trouble
scenarios.tagline: The strongest option is not always the right one.
scenarios.description: A 27-year-old with hay fever wants the strongest antihistamine available. His job — and his chest — should change your answer.
scenarios.mission:
A 27-year-old patient asks for the strongest hay fever treatment you have.

Establish what he actually needs, what he must avoid, and whether anything else deserves attention today.
objectives: Confirm the pattern and severity of allergic rhinitis.
Identify occupational reasons to avoid sedating antihistamines.
Recognise poorly controlled asthma hiding behind hay fever symptoms.
Recommend a non-sedating option with clear counselling.

scenarios.title: The Itchy Rash
scenarios.tagline: Two weeks of itching, and a new hospital placement.
scenarios.description: A 23-year-old student asks for a cream. Distinguishing eczema from infection — and finding the trigger — is the real task.
scenarios.mission:
A 23-year-old patient asks whether you have a cream for an itchy rash.

Assess the rash, exclude infection, find the trigger, and decide what is appropriate to supply.
objectives: Describe the rash: site, appearance, distribution and duration.
Exclude signs of secondary bacterial infection.
Identify the occupational trigger and advise on avoidance.
Counsel on emollient and topical steroid use, including quantity and duration.

scenarios.title: A Parent With a Feverish Child
scenarios.tagline: A worried father, a kitchen teaspoon, and a dose you must get right.
scenarios.description: A three-year-old has had a fever since last night. You need red flags, an accurate weight-based dose, and a parent who leaves knowing exactly what to do.
scenarios.mission:
A father asks what he can give his three-year-old daughter for a fever.

Screen for red flags, establish what has already been given, and make sure the dose leaving this pharmacy is correct and clearly explained.
objectives: Screen systematically for paediatric red flags.
Establish the child’s weight and what has already been administered.
Calculate a correct weight-based paracetamol dose.
Provide safety netting: what to watch for and when to seek urgent help.

scenarios.title: The Patient Who Forgot Their Medication
scenarios.tagline: A week away, three medicines missed.
scenarios.description: A 71-year-old returns from a trip having missed a week of medication. Which omissions matter most, and what should happen today?
scenarios.mission:
A 71-year-old patient tells you she has not taken her tablets for a week.

Find out what was missed, assess the consequences, and agree a safe plan for today.
objectives: Establish exactly which medicines were missed and for how long.
Assess for symptoms and signs of consequence, including hyperglycaemia.
Advise correctly on restarting — without dose doubling.
Decide whether the prescriber needs to be involved, and how urgently.

scenarios.title: The Difficult Inhaler
scenarios.tagline: The inhaler is not failing. The technique is.
scenarios.description: A 19-year-old wants a stronger preventer inhaler. This case is won or lost on how well you can teach.
scenarios.mission:
A 19-year-old patient says her preventer inhaler does not work and asks for something stronger.

Assess her control, her technique and her understanding — then teach in a way she will remember tomorrow.
objectives: Assess asthma control using symptom and reliever-use questions.
Elicit and correct inhaler technique step by step.
Explain the difference between preventer and reliever in plain language.
Check understanding with teach-back, and arrange appropriate follow-up.

scenarios.title: The Unexpected Drug Interaction
scenarios.tagline: “Natural” is not the same as safe.
scenarios.description: A 64-year-old wants St John’s wort. His current medicines make that request a genuine safety event.
scenarios.mission:
A 64-year-old patient asks to buy St John’s wort.

Establish what else he takes, judge the risk, and handle the refusal — if you decide on one — without losing his trust.
objectives: Take a complete medication history, including supplements and herbals.
Identify the interactions with warfarin and sertraline and explain the mechanism.
Assess mood safely, including risk screening.
Redirect to the prescriber while maintaining rapport.

scenarios.title: The Minor Wound
scenarios.tagline: Decide what you can dress — and what you cannot.
scenarios.description: A 29-year-old has cut her palm on a rusty garden fork. Wound assessment, tetanus status and referral thresholds all matter here.
scenarios.mission:
A 29-year-old patient asks you to dress a cut on her palm.

Assess the wound properly, consider contamination and immunisation, and decide whether this belongs in your pharmacy or elsewhere.
objectives: Assess wound size, depth, contamination and neurovascular status.
Establish tetanus immunisation status.
Recognise wounds requiring closure or medical review.
Advise on dressing choice, taking adhesive sensitivity into account.

scenarios.title: The Sore Throat
scenarios.tagline: A common request where the safe answer is not the one being asked for.
scenarios.description: A 19-year-old student asks for antibiotics for a five-day sore throat. Most sore throats are self-limiting — this one has features that change the answer.
scenarios.mission:
A 19-year-old patient asks the pharmacy for antibiotics for a sore throat.

Antibiotics are not a pharmacy supply decision here.

Your job is to establish whether this is self-limiting, needs routine review, or needs same-day assessment.

The features that decide it will not be volunteered.
objectives: Establish duration, severity and fever rather than accepting the request at face value.
Examine or ask about throat appearance and cervical lymph nodes.
Screen actively for airway compromise: difficulty swallowing saliva, drooling, voice change.
Recognise that antibiotic supply is not a pharmacy decision, and explain why.
Refer with a clearly stated urgency and safety-net advice.

scenarios.title: Burning When Passing Urine
scenarios.tagline: A routine request where one unasked question changes the whole answer.
scenarios.description: A 27-year-old asks for something for a bladder infection. Whether this can be managed in the pharmacy depends entirely on a question she has not been asked.
scenarios.mission:
A 27-year-old patient asks for treatment for urinary symptoms.

Some urinary symptoms can be managed in the pharmacy; others cannot.

Establish which this is before deciding anything.

One detail here moves the safe answer completely.
objectives: Characterise the urinary symptoms and their duration.
Screen for systemic features suggesting upper urinary tract involvement.
Establish pregnancy status before considering any treatment.
Recognise that pregnancy moves this out of pharmacy self-care entirely.
Refer appropriately and explain why, without alarming the patient.

scenarios.title: Indigestion, or Something Else
scenarios.tagline: The request is for an antacid. The presentation is not indigestion.
scenarios.description: A 58-year-old asks for something strong for indigestion that started last night. What he describes, once you ask, is not a gastrointestinal problem.
scenarios.mission:
A 58-year-old patient asks for a stronger indigestion remedy.

Chest symptoms in this age group need to be actively characterised before anything is supplied.

Your job is to decide whether this is a pharmacy matter at all.

He will not volunteer the features that decide it.
objectives: Characterise the chest discomfort rather than accepting the patient's own label for it.
Ask specifically about radiation to arm, jaw, neck or back.
Screen for sweating, nausea and breathlessness.
Establish cardiovascular risk factors: age, smoking, blood pressure, family history.
Recognise that this needs emergency assessment, not an antacid.

scenarios.title: The Red Eye
scenarios.tagline: Most red eyes are minor. This one has the features that are not.
scenarios.description: A 31-year-old contact lens wearer asks for conjunctivitis drops. Reduced vision, deep pain and photophobia point somewhere else entirely.
scenarios.mission:
A 31-year-old patient asks for eye drops for what she assumes is conjunctivitis.

Most red eyes are self-limiting; a few threaten sight.

Distinguish between them before supplying anything.

One question about how she corrects her vision changes the risk considerably.
objectives: Establish whether vision is affected, and whether it clears on blinking.
Characterise the pain: surface grittiness versus deep ache with photophobia.
Ask about contact lens wear and overnight use.
Recognise the combination that makes this sight-threatening rather than self-limiting.
Refer for same-day assessment and advise on stopping lens wear.

scenarios.title: A Parent Asking About Teething
scenarios.tagline: Reassurance, an accurate dose, and one product to advise against.
scenarios.description: A tired first-time parent asks what to give a seven-month-old who is teething. The child is well; the risks here are dosing accuracy and the products she has been offered.
scenarios.mission:
A parent asks for something for a seven-month-old who is teething.

Establish that the child is genuinely well before treating anything.

Then get the dose right, and address the products she has already been offered.

How much has already been given is not something she will state precisely.
objectives: Screen for paediatric red flags before accepting teething as the explanation.
Establish the child's current weight for accurate dosing.
Establish exactly what has already been given, and how it was measured.
Advise on the products the parent has been offered, including choking risk.
Counsel on dose, maximum in 24 hours, measurement and when to seek help.
